title: Teaching computers to see the structure of an exam paper
paper_title: HiLEx: Image-Based Hierarchical Layout Extraction from Question Papers
date_note: ICDAR 2025, Wuhan, China, 16-21 Sep 2025 (conference dates from my knowledge of the venue; the PDF is the Springer LNCS version, pp. 485-505)
authors: U Aich, S Chakraborty, D Sadhukhan, Swarnendu Ghosh, T Saha
summary: We built HiLEx, 1,965 labelled pages from eight exams, and tested ten detection models on finding questions, answers and instructions on a page.

body.p: A printed exam paper is full of structure that a person takes in at a glance: questions, answer choices, instructions. A computer looking at a scan sees only pixels. We built HiLEx, a collection of 1,965 exam-paper pages in which six kinds of region are marked by hand. Then we tested ten object detection models on it, to see how well they can find those regions.

Question papers often exist only in hard copy, and well-organised digital question banks are scarce. That makes it hard to pull the questions out automatically. The layouts vary. A page can have one column or several, with instructions and descriptions sitting inside it. On multi-column pages these are often a single line of text squeezed between other sections.

The field that studies this is called document layout analysis: finding the parts of a page and working out what role each one plays. Datasets such as PubLayNet, DocBank, DocLayNet and M6Doc have pushed it forward, but none of them annotates the question and answer structure of an exam page. Even M6Doc, which includes images of test papers, labels standard layout elements instead.

We took pages from eight exams: GMAT, SAT, GRE, GATE, UGC-NET, BANK, JEE and UPSC. Most questions are multiple-choice, though some papers, such as UGC-NET and UPSC, also have descriptive and analytical questions. We used official previous-year papers and free mock exams that are publicly available online, and turned the relevant pages into images. GATE contributes the most pages, 668, and UPSC the fewest, 36 (Table 1).

Each page is labelled with boxes of six kinds. The whole printed area is the Question_Paper_Area. Inside it sit Question_Answer_Blocks, each holding a Question_Block, which is the problem statement, and an Answer_Block, which holds the answer choices or a pre-filled solution. Instruction boxes carry guidelines for the exam or for a set of questions. Description boxes carry explanatory text about an answer.

figure.alt: Two schematic pages, one single-column and one two-column, with coloured boxes nested inside each other and arrows naming the six region types.
figure.caption: The labels are nested like boxes inside boxes, for a single-column page on the left and a two-column page on the right.

body.p: Three expert annotators did the labelling in Roboflow, over two months. They first practised on 10 sample papers. Each also labelled the same 100 shared pages, so that we could measure how well they agreed, using a score called Cohen's kappa. We set the bar at 0.90. The annotations come in two common formats, YOLO and COCO, and the dataset is public on GitHub.

figure.alt: Two annotated exam pages, a single-column page with explanations and a two-column UGC NET page, with coloured rectangles around each region and a colour legend.
figure.caption: Hand-made labels on a single-column page and on a crowded two-column page. Notice how small and tightly packed the answer boxes get.

body.p: We trained ten models from four families. The one-stage detectors, YOLOv8 to YOLOv12, predict all the boxes in a single pass through the network. DETR and RT-DETR are transformer-based. They use self-attention, which lets every part of the image be weighed against every other part. Detectron2 is a two-stage model that first proposes candidate regions and then refines them. Florence-2 and PaLI-Gemma 2 are vision-language models, pretrained on images together with text.

Each model trained for 25 epochs with a batch size of 16, on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. We kept 10% of the pages for testing and split the rest 80:20 into training and validation. The test set has 199 pages with 1,918 labelled regions (Table 3). The main score is mAP50. Roughly, a predicted box counts as a hit if it overlaps the true box enough, and the score averages over the classes. The stricter mAP50-95 averages over overlap thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95.

Large regions are easy. YOLOv8 finds the Question_Paper_Area with an mAP50 of 0.984 (Table 3). Small, rare regions are hard. The test pages hold only 56 Description regions, and the YOLO models reach 0.478 at best on them, with YOLOv12 as low as 0.104 (Table 3). DETR managed 0.071 (Table 4).

figure.alt: Bar chart of mAP50 for five YOLO versions across the six region classes. All versions score high on large regions and low on Description.
figure.caption: Every YOLO version does well on big blocks and badly on Description. YOLOv12 has the lowest bars on Description and Instruction.

body.p: Over all classes, Detectron2 is the best model in our study, with an mAP50 of 0.940 and an mAP50-95 of 0.673 (Table 5). We attribute this to its region proposal network, and we conclude that two-stage models remain the most effective for fine-grained layout understanding. Among the YOLO versions, YOLOv8 has the highest mAP50, 0.848, with YOLOv11 second at 0.822, and YOLOv11 has the highest mAP50-95, 0.689 (Table 3). The vision-language models score 0.835 for PaLI-Gemma 2 and 0.810 for Florence-2 (Table 6). The transformer-based detectors score 0.606 for RT-DETR and 0.502 for DETR (Table 4), and we found them to perform worst overall.

body.callout: Detectron2 reached an mAP50 of 0.940 (Table 5). In our conclusion, Detectron2 performs best, followed by YOLOv11 and PaLI-Gemma 2.

body.p: Looking at the mistakes, we saw two patterns. Some models, among them DETR, Detectron2 and YOLOv12, draw redundant, overlapping boxes. Others, among them YOLOv9 and YOLOv11, miss Instruction and Description regions altogether.

HiLEx has limits that we state in the paper. We removed pages in other languages, so it is English only, and the questions come mostly from Indian national exams, plus GMAT, GRE and SAT. The dataset is unbalanced, as the page counts per exam show (Table 1). It holds page images and boxes, but not yet the text of the questions.

Next we plan to add OCR-based text annotations, so that models that read words and layout together, such as LayoutLMv3, TILT and DocFormer, can be tested. We also plan to add non-English and non-Indian exams, including East Asian, African and European ones.
